title: Preface
summary: The excerpt introduces Thomas H. Davenport and DJ Patil’s 2012 article, which argues that data scientists have become highly sought-after as businesses confront vast and varied data. It illustrates their value through LinkedIn’s Jonathan Goldman, a physicist who analyzed user profiles and connection patterns to identify likely relationships. Despite initial skepticism from engineers focused on scaling the site, CEO Reid Hoffman supported experimentation. Goldman tested personalized “People You May Know” suggestions through ads, refined matching methods using ideas such as triangle closing, and made responding a one-click action. The feature’s click-through rate was 30% higher than other prompts, generated millions of page views, and significantly accelerated LinkedIn’s growth. The excerpt also notes that a shortage of data scientists is constraining some sectors.

title: A New Breed
summary: The passage describes the rise of the data scientist as a high-ranking professional who combines technical training and curiosity to uncover insights from big data. The title was coined in 2008 by DJ Patil and Jeff Hammerbacher, and thousands now work across start-ups and established firms as organizations confront unprecedented data volumes and formats. Companies with petabytes of data, important unstructured information, or questions requiring combined analyses have big-data opportunities. Technologies such as Hadoop and other open-source tools, cloud computing, and data visualization help process this information, but skilled people are just as important. Demand for data scientists exceeds supply, creating a serious constraint in some industries; Greylock Partners has even built a recruiting team to find talent for its portfolio companies. As team leader Dan Portillo notes, businesses need people who can manage data and uncover insights.

title: Who Are These People?
summary: The text explains that hiring data scientists is difficult because the field lacks established degrees, organizational roles, and performance measures. Data scientists turn vast, messy data into useful analysis, discover patterns, communicate findings and business implications, advise leaders, and often develop tools such as Hadoop and Hive. They combine coding, analytical ability, communication and storytelling, creativity, curiosity, experimentation, and business and customer empathy. Successful candidates come from varied computational or data-focused fields—including physical and social sciences, computer science, mathematics, and economics—while traditional analysts or data managers may lack skills for unstructured data or collaboration. Recruiting should assess programming, quantitative foundations, and habits of mind, not statistics alone. Universities and companies are expanding training, while vendors improve tools; examples include EMC’s certification program and the Insight Data Science Fellows Program, which retrains academics through mentoring and practical projects amid strong employer demand. Data scientists also prefer building solutions over merely consulting.

title: Why Would a Data Scientist Want to Work Here?
summary: Data scientists remain in high demand, and candidates weigh roles by the interest and potential for breakthroughs in their data challenges; employers may need to make that potential compelling, especially to candidates from nonbusiness backgrounds. Pay matters, including competitive salaries and stock options, and signals respect and expected business value. More fundamentally, data scientists want to be “on the bridge”—close to unfolding situations and real-time decisions. Though consulting might seem a way to access scarce talent, major firms are only beginning big-data work and often apply their data scientists to conventional quantitative analysis; offshore analytics firms may gain ground. Many data scientists prefer building working solutions to merely advising decision-makers, because creating things offers greater impact and a chance to pioneer the profession.

title: Care and Feeding
summary: Data scientists need freedom to experiment while maintaining close ties to product and service leaders, since their greatest value comes from improving customer-facing products and processes rather than producing executive reports. Examples include Intuit, GE, Google, Zynga, Netflix, and Kaplan, which use data science to develop insights, optimize products and services, improve recommendations, and identify effective learning strategies. Like earlier financial quants, data scientists must also stay connected with specialist communities, internally or externally, to keep skills and tools current; companies should support participation in conferences and associations. Finally, leaders should expect more than basic reporting: despite the challenges of accessing and structuring big data, clear expectations can encourage advanced predictive and optimization work—big data should not mean small math.

title: The Hot Job of the Decade
summary: The text argues that data scientists are highly sought-after because their rare mix of scientific, computational, and analytical skills makes them difficult and costly to hire and retain. It compares them to early financial quants and search engineers, whose once-specialized skills later became more widely available through university programs. Firms might consider waiting for a larger, more affordable generation of data scientists, leaving early recruitment to big-data startups and aggressive companies such as GE and Walmart. However, because big data’s growth shows no sign of slowing, delaying risks allowing competitors and partners to gain lasting advantages; companies need skilled people to capitalize on the emerging trend. The text identifies the article as a version published in Harvard Business Review in October 2012 and provides biographical information about coauthors Thomas H. Davenport and DJ Patil, along with related topics and a link.
